title: Jewish Renewal
hook: Zalman Schachter-Shalomi joined Hasidic spirituality with egalitarian openness

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: many ways to picture God. Kaplan's God was a power in the world that makes for goodness, one picture among several. Whom did you ask, and what did they say? Today, a movement built around how people pray. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

The chairs are pushed into a circle, not rows. Someone starts a melody with no words, just a sound, and it goes around once, twice, ten times, until the whole room is carrying it. A woman leads the next prayer. A man near the window is swaying with his eyes closed. Then the room drops into silence, a long one, before the Hebrew begins again. Some of what happens here would be at home in a Hasidic study house. Some of it would surprise the people praying there. The rabbi whose life made rooms like this possible was Zalman Schachter-Shalomi, called Reb Zalman by the people who learned from him. His movement is today's word.
screen: `A CIRCLE OF CHAIRS.` → `A MELODY WITH NO WORDS.` → `THEN, SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Jewish Renewal. Its roots first. Reb Zalman was formed in Hasidism, in the Chabad world, where prayer is meant to be felt as well as said: the wordless melody called a niggun, the joy, the long gathering around a rebbe's table. The Psalm says it plainly: "Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing." Then came the opening. He carried that warmth to people who would never have walked into a Hasidic synagogue, and in Renewal communities women and men lead prayer, teach and serve as rabbis side by side. Look at the forms. Renewal gatherings may chant one line again and again until it settles, sit in silent meditation, move, sing in Hebrew and English, and pray with the body as well as the book. Reb Zalman cared about the craft of prayer the way a musician cares about practice: how to make the words land in a living person. Finally, what the name points to. In the traditional service, as the Torah scroll goes back into the ark, the congregation sings a verse from Lamentations: "renew our days as of old." Renewal in that verse is not novelty. It is going back to a source to find it fresh. That is the hope Renewal communities name. Other Jews ask real questions in return: how far new forms can stretch, and how binding halakha remains inside them. Renewal Jews hold a range of answers on that, too. The same verse is sung in Renewal circles and in Hasidic study houses, and each reads it in its own way.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try one new prayer form. Settle, and breathe. Choose a single line and give it the whole sit. If you pray, you can take a line you already know, say "Serve the LORD with gladness," and repeat it slowly on the out-breath, letting it become quieter each time, until it is almost only breath. If you don't pray, hum one simple tune with no words, over and over, and let it slow down. When your mind wanders, come back to the line or the tune. No performance. Nobody is listening but you. The bell holds the time.
Jewish Renewal. The movement shaped by Reb Zalman Schachter-Shalomi: Hasidic warmth and prayer craft, opened to everyone, with women and men leading equally. Today's word.
Your line: renewal. Today, do one familiar thing slowly and on purpose, a blessing, a greeting, a cup of tea, as if it were new. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.
